items.title: Guidance on AI and data protection: How do we ensure individual rights in our AI systems?
items.locator: Section 'What is the role of human oversight?', subsection 'How should we train our staff to address these risks?'
items.quote: This authority and confidence cannot be created by policies and training alone: a supportive organisational culture is also crucial
items.why: Source of the quotation. Says reviewers must have authority to override and confidence they will not be penalised, that training must be kept up to date with refresher sessions, and that risk and internal audit may also need training. The page carries the banner that the guidance is under review because of the Data (Use and Access) Act; page metadata date 31 March 2026.

items.title: Data protection audit framework, Artificial intelligence toolkit: Human review
items.locator: First control measure and its 'ways to meet our expectations' list
items.quote: Assign human reviewers a manageable caseload and ensure there is sufficient resource in place for them to give appropriate time to their tasks.
items.why: What the regulator's auditors look for: reviewers with knowledge, experience, authority and independence; a manageable caseload; a log of overrides with reasons; reporting lines in job descriptions. Carries the 'under review' banner; page metadata date 20 November 2024.

items.title: Automated decision-making, including profiling: What does the UK GDPR say about ADM?
items.locator: Section 'What is a 'solely' automated decision?', list of criteria for meaningful human involvement
items.quote: be suitably trained and qualified to understand the system’s logic, outputs, limitations, and risks; and
items.why: Consultation draft (updated 31 March 2026), not final guidance. Makes the reviewer's training and qualification one of the criteria for human involvement to count as meaningful under UK GDPR Article 22A, and says ad hoc spot checks are not enough.

items.title: Explaining decisions made with AI, Part 2, Task 5: Prepare implementers to deploy your AI system
items.publisher: Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute
items.locator: 'At a glance' and the passage on decision-automation bias
items.quote: This means that they need to be appropriately trained to use the model’s results responsibly and fairly.
items.why: Sets out what system-specific preparation of the people who act on AI output should cover, including the two opposite errors of over-trusting and distrusting the system. Page metadata date 19 November 2024.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: Deployers shall assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, as well as the necessary support.
items.why: The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). The page carries a notice that the provision was amended by the Digital Omnibus and the text shown is not yet updated; paragraph 2 is not marked as amended on the page. High-risk systems only.

items.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 113: Entry into force and application
items.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
items.quote: 2 December 2027 as regards AI systems classified as high-risk pursuant to Article 6(2) and Annex III; and
items.why: Source of the application date in the brief for the deployer oversight duty (Chapter III, Section 3). The Commission's copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page, HTTP 202). The page shows amended text under 'AMENDED' labels beside a banner saying the text is not yet updated; the Commission's timeline page gives the same date.

items.title: AI Literacy - Questions & Answers
items.locator: Answer to 'Is an AI training mandatory for article 4 of the AI Act or are other AI literacy initiatives also allowed?'
items.quote: Relying on the instructions of use is therefore not sufficient, further measures are necessary.
items.why: The Commission's reading of Article 26: deployers of high-risk systems must ensure the staff handling the system are sufficiently trained to ensure human oversight, and that duty was kept when the general literacy duty was softened in 2026. Not binding.

items.title: The flaws of policies requiring human oversight of government algorithms
items.publisher: Ben Green, Computer Law & Security Review 45 (author's copy on arXiv)
items.quote: I survey 41 policies that prescribe human oversight of government algorithms and find that they suffer from two significant flaws.
items.why: Source of the figure. Peer-reviewed (Computer Law & Security Review 45, 105681); read on arXiv, where the author deposited it, because the publisher's page returned no text to a plain request. Argues that people are often unable to do the oversight asked of them and that naming an overseer can give false assurance. About government algorithms; the lesson is applied to companies by analogy.

items.title: On the Quest for Effective Human Oversight: Legal, Philosophical, and Technical Perspectives
items.publisher: Sarah Sterz and others, ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2024 (authors' copy on arXiv)
items.quote: (a) sufficient causal power with regard to the system and its effects, (b) suitable epistemic access to relevant aspects of the situation
items.why: A cross-disciplinary account of what makes an overseer effective: power to change the outcome, access to the relevant facts, self-control and fitting intentions, shaped by system design, the individual and the working environment. Abstract read; conceptual, no data.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.quote: Processes for operator and practitioner proficiency with AI system performance and trustworthiness
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary US framework that asks for operator proficiency to be defined, assessed and documented, and for oversight roles to be set out in policy.

items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 5.1: Skills, knowledge and expertise (competent employees rule)
items.locator: SYSC 5.1.1R (text shown as in force from 23/10/2025)
items.quote: A firm must employ personnel with the skills, knowledge and expertise necessary for the discharge of the responsibilities allocated to them.
items.why: A binding UK rule on the competence of the person: a regulated firm that allocates oversight of an AI system to someone must be able to show that person has the skills for it. Limits: applies to FCA-authorised firms only; a general rule that does not mention AI or human oversight; the Handbook page says SYSC 5.1 was last updated on 09/12/2025.

items.title: Supervisory Statement SS1/23: Model risk management principles for banks
items.publisher: Prudential Regulation Authority, Bank of England
items.quote: Roles and responsibilities should be allocated to staff with appropriate skills and experience to ensure the MRM framework operates effectively.
items.why: The prudential regulator's expectation that those who challenge and monitor models have documented skills, experience, independence and seniority for the role; Principle 4 adds independent, effective challenge. Limits: banks, building societies and designated investment firms only; covers models generally, including AI; in effect from 17 May 2024.

items.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
items.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division), via The National Archives Find Case Law
items.quote: We do not consider the "human failsafe" is sufficient to discharge the PSED.
items.why: The Court of Appeal declined to treat a human check on each facial recognition match as an answer to the duty to investigate possible bias in the software, noting that human beings also make mistakes. Shows that the presence of an overseer does not by itself discharge the organisation's own duty. Limits: decided on the public sector equality duty and police use of live facial recognition; not a ruling on reviewer training.

items.title: Institutionalised distrust and human oversight of artificial intelligence: towards a democratic design of AI governance under the European Union AI Act
items.quote: They may be lacking in competence or be harmfully incentivised.
items.why: Peer-reviewed, open access. Names the two failure points this criterion tests, competence and incentives, and argues the EU Act says little on how to make oversight effective; proposes principles that assume overseers are fallible. Limits: legal and conceptual analysis, not an empirical study; written about the EU Act before its 2026 amendment; abstract was the passage read.

items.title: Human-AI Interactions in Public Sector Decision-Making: "Automation Bias" and "Selective Adherence" to Algorithmic Advice
items.publisher: Alon-Barkat and Busuioc; Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory (author copy on arXiv, v3)
items.quote: We find a stronger propensity for adherence when the advice is aligned with group stereotypes
items.why: Three experiments (605, 904 and 1,345 participants, the last with civil servants) on how decision-makers treat algorithmic advice. A caution against a single story: the authors did not find automation bias, but in one study found advice was followed more readily when it matched stereotypes. Limits: the Netherlands; survey experiments, not live casework; the arXiv listing says it was published in the journal in 2022, and the author copy was read, not the publisher's.

items.title: Moral Crumple Zones: Cautionary Tales in Human-Robot Interaction
items.publisher: Elish; Engaging Science, Technology, and Society, Vol. 5 (2019)
items.quote: responsibility for an action may be misattributed to a human actor who had limited control over the behavior of an automated or autonomous system
items.why: Open access journal article behind the brief's point that the overseer carries blame for outcomes they could not change: the nearest human absorbs moral and legal responsibility when an automated system fails. Limits: case studies of accidents (aviation, self-driving cars) and their media coverage, not a measured effect; US; abstract was the passage read.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Suggested action MS-4.2-004; GOVERN 3.2 on roles for human-AI configurations and oversight
items.quote: Monitor and document instances where human operators or other systems override the GAI's decisions.
items.why: A standard-setter's version of the measure the framework's higher levels expect: record and evaluate overrides. The profile also treats automation bias and over-reliance as a named risk ('Human-AI Configuration'). Limits: voluntary; US; generative AI only; a different document from the AI RMF 1.0 already on the list.
